summary: Defines an extension to the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) to support the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol for IPv4 (ILNPv4). It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

eli5.summary: ARP is how a computer asks who has this address so it can deliver mail. This memo teaches that question a few new tricks needed by ILNP. It is only an experiment.

questions: what are the arp operation codes for ilnpv4
how does ilnpv4 arp differ from standard arp
why does ilnpv4 need arp extensions
subtitle: Extensions to ARP that let it carry ILNP identifiers and locators.

tldr.problem: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IPv4 addresses to hardware addresses. ILNP splits the address concept into a Locator (which is like an IPv4 address) and an Identifier (which is unique to the node). Standard ARP only knows about IPv4 addresses and cannot carry Identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: Two new ARP operation codes (24 and 25, for experimental use) extend the ARP Request and Reply to carry both 32-bit Locators and 64-bit Node Identifiers alongside the existing hardware addresses.
tldr.outcome: This proposal demonstrates that the common ILNP architecture can be implemented with different network-layer protocols by extending existing mechanisms like ARP.

today: RFC 6747 is an Experimental protocol from the IRTF Routing Research Group published in November 2012. It remains experimental and has not been adopted for deployment.

sections.title: Why ILNP Needs ARP Extensions
sections.content:
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is how computers on a local network ask "who has IP address X?" Standard IPv4 ARP maps 32-bit IPv4 addresses to 48-bit Ethernet hardware addresses.

ILNP separates addressing into two concepts: a Locator (topology-dependent, used for routing) and an Identifier (topology-independent, naming the node itself). For ILNPv4, the Locator is the same size as an IPv4 address (32 bits), but the Identifier is 64 bits and cannot fit in the IPv4 header itself.

When an ILNP node needs to discover the hardware address of a peer on a local network, it cannot use standard ARP because ARP packets are not large enough to carry both the Locator and the Identifier. ILNP therefore defines extended ARP operation codes that can carry both pieces of information.
sections.eli5: When your computer wants to talk to another computer nearby, it first asks "who has address 10.1.1.5?" ILNP ARP also asks "and what is your real name (Identifier)?"

sections.title: The ILNPv4 ARP Request
sections.content:
The ILNPv4 ARP Request extends the standard ARP Request (operation code 1) using experimental operation code 24. Unlike standard ARP, it carries:

  • S_L32: The sender's 32-bit Locator (same as a normal IPv4 source address in ARP).
  • S_NID: The sender's 64-bit Node Identifier (8 bytes).
  • T_L32: The target's 32-bit Locator (what the ARP Request is asking for).
  • T_NID: The target's 64-bit Node Identifier (what the ARP Request is asking for).
  • Hardware fields: Source hardware address (S_HA) and target hardware address (T_HA), as in standard ARP.

The Protocol Address Length (PAL) field uses a new value of 12 (instead of 4 for IPv4 ARP), indicating that addresses are now 12 octets long: 4 for the Locator plus 8 for the Identifier.

The operation code 24 signals that this is an ILNP ARP Request, not a standard IPv4 ARP Request.
sections.eli5: The request says: "I am sender-name at sender-address 10.1.1.5, looking for target-name at target-address 10.1.1.6. What is your hardware address?"

sections.title: The ILNPv4 ARP Reply
sections.content:
The ILNPv4 ARP Reply extends the standard ARP Reply (operation code 2) using experimental operation code 25. The reply has the same extended structure as the request, containing all four fields (S_L32, S_NID, T_L32, T_NID) and hardware addresses.

The semantics are identical to standard ARP: the sender of the reply is confirming that it owns the L32 and NID values specified in the reply message, and is providing its hardware address. The target fields echo back information from the request to close the address resolution loop.

When an ILNP ARP reply is received, the receiving node learns the mapping between the target's Locator, Identifier, and hardware address, and it caches this information.
sections.eli5: The reply says: "Yes, I am target-name at target-address 10.1.1.6, and my hardware address is AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF."

sections.title: How ILNPv4 ARP Works
sections.content:
The operation of ILNPv4 ARP is almost identical to standard IPv4 ARP, with these key differences:

  • Use operation code 24 for ARP Requests instead of 1.
  • Use operation code 25 for ARP Replies instead of 2.
  • Include both L32 (Locator) and NID (Identifier) values in both requests and replies.
  • Set Protocol Address Length to 12 instead of 4.

Nodes should be able to implement this by extending existing ARP code rather than writing entirely new code. Because codes 24 and 25 are shared experimental values (from RFC 5494), other experiments might also use these codes. Implementations should code defensively and validate that received ARP messages actually conform to the ILNP ARP format they expect.
sections.eli5: It is almost exactly like normal ARP on a local network, but with more information (both the address and the real name) in each message.

sections.title: Security Implications and Mitigations
sections.content:
Standard ARP has no authentication mechanism, making it vulnerable to on-link attackers who can forge ARP packets to steal addresses or perform man-in-the-middle attacks. RFC 5227 describes these risks and some detection methods.

ILNPv4 ARP does not change these fundamental security properties. An on-link attacker can still forge ARP messages claiming to own any Identifier or Locator. However, the use of distinct operation codes (24 and 25 instead of 1 and 2) at least prevents an attacker from spoofing legitimate IPv4 ARP to confuse ILNP nodes.

For high-risk environments, IEEE 802.1 AE (link-layer security) SHOULD be deployed to provide cryptographic authentication of ARP messages at the link layer.
sections.eli5: Someone on your local network can lie and say they own an address, just like with normal ARP. Link-layer encryption can prevent this if you need strong security.

sections.title: Implementation and Interoperability
sections.content:
Implementations must understand that operation codes 24 and 25 are shared experimental values. Different experiments on the same local network could use these codes for entirely different purposes, leading to confusion or packet misinterpretation.

The field definitions marked with an asterisk in the RFC should have the same meanings as in standard IPv4 ARP. The main difference is that the address fields now carry both a 32-bit Locator and a 64-bit Identifier instead of a single 32-bit IPv4 address.

This is an experimental protocol from the IRTF Routing Research Group. If the IETF were to standardize ILNP, unique ARP operation codes would be allocated as part of that process.
sections.eli5: Programmers need to be careful when implementing this, because other experiments might use codes 24 and 25 for different things.

fields.name: Hardware Type
fields.desc: Same as IPv4 ARP (e.g., 1 for Ethernet)

fields.name: Protocol Type
fields.desc: Same as IPv4 ARP (e.g., 0x0800 for IPv4)

fields.name: Hardware Address Length
fields.desc: Same as IPv4 ARP (e.g., 6 for Ethernet)

fields.name: Protocol Address Length
fields.desc: New value: 12 (4 bytes Locator + 8 bytes Identifier)

fields.name: Sender Hardware Address
fields.desc: Same as IPv4 ARP (e.g., Ethernet MAC)

fields.name: Target Hardware Address
fields.desc: Target's hardware address (or zero in request)

fields.name: Target L32
fields.desc: Target's 32-bit Locator (what we are asking for)
